stories.title: Man jailed for life for murder of Waterford woman in 2025
stories.summary: The family of Waterford woman Gillian Curran have said that the sentencing of her killer is a step towards justice, but they want to make sure the voices of all victims of domestic abuse are heard and that no one is forgotten. The Curran family made the comments outside the Criminal Courts of Justice in Dublin after 36-year-old Marcus O'Neill was handed the mandatory life sentence for murder. Ms Curran, who was 47 and originally from Sweetbriar in Tramore, was found unresponsive at her partner’s house on the morning of 25 January 2025 and pronounced dead a short time later. O’Neill had denied murdering Ms Curran at his home on O'Brien Street in Waterford city. However, in July, a jury of five men and seven women returned a majority 10-2 verdict and found him guilty of murder. The trial at the Central Criminal Court in Waterford marked the first time that footage from a garda body cam was used as evidence in criminal proceedings.

stories.title: O'Neill survives confidence motion over Garvaghy protests
stories.summary: Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill has survived a motion to remove her from office for standing with the protesters blocking the Orange Order parade on the Garvaghy Road in Portadown two weeks ago. The TUV party motion was defeated, getting only 34 of 70 votes and no nationalist votes, falling well short of the cross-community support required from a majority of both unionist and nationalist MLAs to remove a minister. During a 3-hour debate, Sinn Fein MLAs defended Ms O'Neill, while a number of unionist assembly members called for the DUP to remove Emma Little Pengelly as Deputy First Minister, which would also trigger the removal of the First Minister. Michelle O'Neill said "the Orange state is gone forever" as she responded to the motion of no confidence in the Stormont assembly. Ms O'Neill's Sinn Féin colleagues, Finance Minister John O'Dowd, Economy Minister Caoimhe Archibald and Infrastructure Minister Liz Kimmins, are also facing no confidence motions after backing Garvaghy Road residents amid the protests. The First Minister was among a number of people who received a letter from the PSNI to be interviewed over alleged offences around the protests.

stories.title: Will the Government's new investment account work for you?
stories.summary: Analysis: Whether the new investment account is attractive to you will depend on a number of factors, including your demographic and ambitions Minister for Finance Simon Harris announced in Budget 2027 that the Irish Investment Account will open for business on 1 July 2027. Up to €12,000 a year can be invested through the account, with no minimum amount. The money can go into shares, bonds, investment funds, exchange traded funds (ETFs) or insurance-based investment products, but not crypto. There are no limits on where the money is invested, so, despite the European Commission's aims for accounts of this kind, much of it may flow to US and other global companies rather than European ones. Anyone aged 18 or over, resident in Ireland and with a PPS number can open one. The first €50,000 is tax free and the investor pays tax of 1% a year on the part over €50,000. The Minister for Finance's own example was an account worth €52,000, which would pay €20 tax for the year. This is based on the account's value not its profit, so a saver could pay tax in a year when their investments did not grow at all. The upside is that the usual taxes on investing do not apply. Profits on most funds outside of this account are taxed at 38%, falling to 35% in January, and deemed disposal taxes funds every eight years even if they are not sold. None of this applies to the new account. The provider handles all the tax and pays it to Revenue on the saver's behalf, so the saver does not have to work out or return any tax. Can savers get at the money? Yes. There is no lock-in and no minimum term. Whether money can be taken out and put back in the same year, without using up that year's allowance, has not been said. What's the limit and is it fair? €12,000 a year, or €1,000 a month, which is well below Britain's £20,000 limit, so it's less of a tax break for the very wealthy. Still, few households can put aside €1,000 a month easily, so the benefit will flow mostly to people who already save.

stories.title: Riyadh airport closure extended after Houthi attacks
stories.summary: Saudi authorities have extended the suspension of operations at Riyadh's international airport following a series of deadly Houthi attacks. Recent strikes on the airport have killed at least 18 people, including 13 on Saturday in the deadliest attack on the country in more than a decade, which also left hundreds wounded. An Irish national, who was caught up in the attack, said he was "lucky to be alive". The General Authority of Civil Aviation in a statement announced "the extension of the suspension of operations at King Khalid International Airport". It said the extension was needed to "complete the necessary procedures to verify the safety of the facilities and their operational readiness". A senior aviation source who oversees flights to the Gulf for an airline said operations would be halted for the remainder of the working week in Saudi Arabia, according to messages sent to the carrier from Saudi aviation authorities.

stories.title: Loughlin proud as testing journey ultimately ends in joy
stories.summary: The Downs' joint-captain Luke Loughlin has said that missing out on Westmeath’s historic year helped him develop a greater perspective on life – and also lit a fire in him to help his club retain the Flanagan Cup. Lake County boss Mark McHugh was in attendance as Loughlin’s seven points helped the side to a dramatic 1-18 to 0-20 win over St Loman’s. In April, Loughlin was forced off the county scene due to a hamstring tear and tendon rupture. It meant that Westmeath were short one key forward, but they managed to overcome that in a famous manner as they claimed just a second-ever Leinster title with an extra-time win over Dublin. Unavailable for that triumph, Loughlin instead put his full focus on club matters and it paid off handsomely at TEG Cusack Park on Sunday. "When it happened I just said, and it’s documented, that I wasn’t going to be playing. "We probably let ourselves down in Leinster a little last year [losing a quarter-final to Offaly champions Tullamore].

stories.summary: The SSE Airtricity Men's Premier Division title race enters its final few furlongs at Tallaght Stadium tonight and a faller four out could see Shamrock Rovers or Bohemians lose the momentum to get over the line. Every game is crucial in this three-way battle – St Pat's able to sit back and watch from afar ahead of Friday’s game against Shelbourne – and defeat for Bohs in particular would surely spell the end game for their hopes of landing a first title since 2009. Alan Reynolds’ side trail Rovers by three points yet any sort of win would see them move top for four days at least. Rovers, by contrast, are well used to these high-pressure situations as they chase a sixth title in seven years. Most of those were won with relative ease, but they did have to fend off a late Derry surge last year, and manager Stephen Bradley feels that banked experience could be crucial. "What’s great about the group is we have real experience built up in understanding what it takes to go the long haul in a season," he said. "We’ve done it for so long. What comes with that is real trust and belief and understanding. Trust the process in what we do.

stories.title: Cullen wants more from Leinster after 'disjointed' win
stories.summary: Leinster head coach Leo Cullen wasn't getting carried away by his side's 29-5 win against Cardiff at Laya Arena, insisting the province will have to get better after what he described as a "disjointed" performance. The defending URC champions marked their first game at the newly redeveloped RDS by scoring five tries to one against the Welsh side, as they held Cardiff at arm’s length to register their first win of the season, in front of a near sold out crowd of 20,035 people. At half time, it looked like Leinster were set to pull away from Corniel van Zyl’s side, leading 22-5 with a bonus-point already secure. However, a sloppy third quarter meant they spent much of the second half defending, before a late Jamie Osborne try killed things off. "Up and running" was how Cullen summed things up after the 24-point victory, but while he was pleased to pick up a first win of the season - with nine of the starting team making their first appearances of the season - he was far from delighted. "Lots of good stuff in the first half. Unfortunately, at the start of the second half we don't put on much of a show, it gets a bit disjointed.

Saturday Night Live has become an institution of television since its premiere in 1975 - and with the launch of SNL UK last year, there are now arguably even more relevant cultural touchpoints for Irish viewers. There have been many Irish guests and musical acts on the variety show over the years, most recently with CMAT appearing as the musical performer alongside Jeff Goldblum on SNL UK in September. But while some have embraced the opportunity to poke fun at themselves and their Irishness, others have produced moments that have landed rather less successfully… For all its comedic and writing talent, SNL has customarily gone for the low-hanging fruit when it comes to writing sketches for Irish guests: drinking, fighting, singing, potatoes, making fun of our accent and generally embracing every lazy stereotype you can imagine. However, Paul Mescal did his bit to level the score by taking the mick out of Americans in this 2024 sketch (which was cut for time on the day of broadcast, but later made available online.) Mescal plays a barman in an Irish pub who is astounded to learn of that rare phenomenon: an American tourist claiming Irish ancestry. Someone cast this man in a comedy, stat. This sketch was a great example of how to be funny without necessarily punching down - and in this case, it felt like SNL was laughing with us, not at us. Here, a cast that included Kate McKinnon, Cecily Strong, Aidy Bryant and actress Anya Taylor-Joy (with an impressive accent, it must be said), skewered the 'mythical Ireland' trope pushed by the likes of Celtic Woman. There are some top-notch lines here, including ‘Witness Irish culture the best way it was meant to be enjoyed… in Ohio’ and ‘If you liked Riverdance but wished they could move their arms, you’ll love us.’’ Several of the original Celtic Woman members took it in good humour, with Chloe Agnew claiming that SNL had "nailed it." There wasn't a single Irish person in this sketch, which perhaps is what makes it successful as there’s no caricature to poke fun at. The 'Irish play’ in question is a fictional production called The Storm Within by Rory McFaddin (that well-known playwright) which is experiencing problems due to its promise of nudity, the cast coming down with Covid, and terrible understudies that need to be fed their lines. Selena Gomez attempts to do an Irish accent and quickly gives up, diverting to Australian; Kenan Thompson is the play’s harried director and there’s an ending that is actually funny.

stories.title: Selma Blair pleads not guilty to assault charges
stories.summary: Actress Selma Blair has pleaded not guilty to two counts of assault following an alleged disturbance aboard a flight from Los Angeles to New York. The 54-year-old Legally Blonde and Cruel Intentions star appeared in court in Queens on Monday, charged over alleged assaults on a police officer and a nurse after the plane landed. According to court documents, Blair allegedly kicked the officer while being restrained on a stretcher and later kicked a nurse at a New York hospital. Blair was detained at John F Kennedy Airport late on Sunday following reports of a physically abusive passenger aboard a Delta Air Lines flight. Two cabin crew members reported injuries, with one taken to hospital for evaluation. The FBI has also issued Blair with a summons relating to allegations of assault aboard the aircraft, according to a federal law enforcement official cited by the Associated Press.

stories.title: Bláthnaid Ní Chofaigh: 'I don't plan to go anywhere'
stories.summary:
For Bláthnaid Ní Chofaigh, the death of her younger sister, Bríd, has taken so much. But the memories are still vivid and enriching. Donal O'Donoghue meets her. "The stories I hear and the people I meet through Nationwide are therapeutic," says Bláthnaid Ní Chofaigh of how work has helped since her sister, Bríd, died from cervical cancer in January last year, shortly after her 42nd birthday. But grief can catch her still. "I came out of dubbing the other day, happy, and I just started singing 'With your long blonde hair and your eyes blue’ from David Bowie’s ‘Sorrow’ and then I put my hand on the wall and stopped because I thought of Bríd. Sometimes when I feel joy I feel guilt. It was my baby sister; she shouldn’t have died. Hopefully, the next time I’m talking to you that will have passed." Her eyes well. "She was 42 when she died and was 38 when she was diagnosed. For four years she suffered. I watched Bríd on trial drugs. She grabbed at everything to survive. And on the night that she was failing, I just knew. It’s probably the most useless you ever feel, watching someone die because there’s nothing you can do." What helps? "Being with my mother, Áine, is a huge connection to Bríd," she says. "Bríd was her last baby. Jaysus, nobody expected her (Bríd, the youngest of five, was born 10 years after her four siblings) and she wanted for nothing. If she was here now, she’d probably be having a glass of Prosecco. ‘She had notions’ as they might say down the country. "And she had a great relationship with our mother. Like yesterday, I was helping mum with her make-up – she’s 88 but still in great form – and whatever way she looked at me as I put on her eyeliner we both
burst out laughing. That moment with my mother connected me to Bríd. And I love talking about Bríd now.

stories.title: Govt to hear of strike impact on economy, smaller firms
stories.summary: Government ministers are to hear warnings of the impact of tomorrow's public sector strike on the wider economy, particularly smaller businesses, as parents are forced to take leave to look after children. In a memo to the Cabinet, Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers will outline some of the other anticipated impacts of the strike, including the cancellation of outpatient hospital appointments and non-emergency procedures as well as the closure of most schools, colleges and universities. stories.title: Union leaders reject minister's plea to postpone strikes
stories.summary: Union leaders have said a letter from Public Expenditure Minister Jack Chambers urging them to call off Wednesday's planned public sector strike "does not represent any change in his previously stated position". In a statement, the Public Services Committee of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions (ICTU) said unions continue to prepare for a 24-hour work stoppage that will take place on Wednesday. In response to Mr Chambers, the union leaders said that the Government must acknowledge that the specific pay issues raised by unions will be addressed in any talks at the outset. They also stressed the importance of restoring confidence in the public service industrial relations process, saying it has been "severely damaged" by unimplemented commitments in the last agreement. Minister Chambers wrote to trade union leaders stating that "pay issues can and should be discussed as a priority alongside other matters as part of the pay talks." In the letter, Mr Chambers urged ICTU to postpone the strike action scheduled for Wednesday to allow for "urgent and intensive engagement to get underway tomorrow at the Workplace Relations Commission".

stories.title: Wednesday Dáil sitting cancelled over strike action
stories.summary: The Dáil will not sit next Wednesday due to the public sector strike day, in a move the opposition is describing as a climbdown by the government. Instead of the usual three-day schedule, the lower house will only meet on Tuesday and Thursday next week. Committee and Seanad business are also cancelled for Wednesday. The Government had initially pushed for the Dáil to go ahead on Wednesday with a suggestion that unions might give officials a derogation. Opposition party members had insisted they would not cross picket lines. No derogation was agreed, and government chief whip Mary Butler today tabled a revised schedule for Tuesday and Thursday of next week only.

stories.title: Greencore upgrades its full year profit guidance again
stories.summary: Ireland-headquartered convenience food manufacturer Greencore has again upgraded its full year adjusted operating profit guidance after it said it had ended its fiscal year strongly, with volume growth ahead of the market, "excellent" profit momentum and positive cashflow generation. It said it now anticipates its full year adjusted operating profit for continuing operations to be about £248m, ahead of current market expectations and previously raised guidance. In a trading update for the fourth quarter to the end of September, Greencore said its fourth quarter revenue increased 4.5% to £1.036 billion. It said this reflected strong volume growth and recovery of labour, packaging and certain raw materials inflation. In January, the London-listed firm acquired fellow supermarket supplier Bakkavor with the deal forming the UK's leading manufacturer of fresh convenience foods. Bakkavor's retail customers include Tesco, Marks & Spencer and Waitrose, while Greencore supplies all major UK supermarkets and is the biggest pre-packed sandwich maker in the UK.

stories.title: Kyiv says Russia hit energy targets despite Trump truce
stories.summary: Russia hit at least six energy targets during a night and morning of deadly airstrikes across Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said, adding this showed Moscow had no interest in an energy ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump. Under ⁠pressure over high energy prices ahead of US midterm elections next month, Mr Trump declared that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to hit each other's energy systems. "It is increasingly evident that Russia is unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire proposed by the United States and intends to continue its terrorist air attacks against our people and communities," Mr Zelensky said on X. "This is what happens when Russia sees the prospect of higher revenues for its war machine," he added. In earlier comments by video link to a conference in Poland, Mr Zelensky identified two of the targets as a gas facility and a petrol station, both hit by Russian drones. Mr Trump announced the purported energy ceasefire days after unveiling a deal to buy diesel from Russia, which Mr Zelensky has criticised as a reversal of years of Western policy aimed at isolating Russia's economy.

stories.title: Issues remain up front as Ulster strive for consistency
stories.summary: Interprovincial matches are always tightly contested and Saturday's meeting between Munster and Ulster was no exception. Despite Munster racing into a commanding lead, the game finished on a knife-edge, with both sides trying to clinch the all-important winning score. Ulster have endured an awkward start to the season. A high-scoring draw away against Glasgow should be seen as a very respectable result. In their other two fixtures they chased down sizable deficits to draw with Munster and come within a score of a comeback win against Edinburgh. It is hardly the start Richie Murphy would have wanted as the province look to re-establish themselves in the top eight of the United Rugby Championship and secure their place among Europe’s elite. It’s also not the start to a match that the head coach of any team would want. Murphy spoke afterwards about their aim to start fast but Ulster let themselves down in the first 40 in Belfast. They have no problem scoring points in the second half of matches. It was a simple equation for Murphy, focus on the start and the rest will look after itself. That was not to be as Munster destroyed the hosts' setpiece and forced many errors in the Ulster attack. Kieran Brookes has been a surprise package for the Munster scrum. Aided by player of the match, Marnus Van Der Merwe, the visitors turned over an Ulster scrum against the feed to assert their scrum dominance over the northern province in the early stages of the game.
stories.rssSummary: After a patchy start to the season, it's clear that Ulster's problems currently lie in the fundamentals and the basics of their forwards game.

stories.title: Inagh-Kilnamona come good to be crowned Clare champions
stories.summary: Inagh-Kilnamona outscored neighbours Kilmaley by 1-06 to 0-02 in the last quarter to finally cement their first-ever Clare Senior Hurling Championship crown in Zimmer Biomet Páirc Chiosóg in Ennis. Only permanently amalgamating in 2008, Inagh-Kilnamona had to wait patiently before eventually becoming the tenth different club in that period to lift the famed Canon Hamilton trophy. However, it would be more than worth the wait as their superior spread of leaders finally got Eugene Cullinan's side over the line. Kilmaley had eight different scorers but none of those could match the scoring feats of Aidan McCarthy and Fred Hegarty who grabbed 1-05 each while two-time All-Star David Fitzgerald also raided for five points, three of which would be the catalyst for that match-winning final flourish. After all, amidst such an anxious and cagey wrestle for supremacy, the neighbours would be deadlocked for the sixth time entering the final ten minutes at 1-12 to 1-12. However, it was Fitzgerald who put daylight between the sides while captain Aidan McCarthy, playmaker Sean Rynne and substitute Niall Mullins also got in on the scoring action before Fred Hegarty fired a clinching 63rd-minute goal to put the result beyond any doubt.

stories.title: Manchester City sweep past 10-man Liverpool at Anfield
stories.summary: Uncertainty may surround Manchester City's future but nothing changed for them on the pitch as the Premier League leaders successfully came through their first public examination since being found guilty by an independent commission. Having been subjected to a febrile atmosphere at Anfield where they were labelled cheats and booed at every opportunity Enzo Maresca’s side shrugged off the slurs relating to the numerous breaches of financial rules to win 3-0. The way they brushed off the taunts was similar to the way the club, who have lodged an appeal, have treated the decision of the independent commission and the fact it was business as usual showed there appears to be no visible concerns from the players when it comes to delivering on the pitch. Erling Haaland made the crucial breakthrough in front his father Alfe-Inge stood – with the away fans waving their throwback inflatable yellow bananas – just three minutes after Ryan Gravenberch was sent off for a second bookable offence, both soft yellow cards. Subsitute Jeremy Doku, who helped turn the game the visitors’ way after coming on in the 56th minute, curled home a second and Rayan Cherki rolled in a third to allow Maresca the luxury of resting Haaland with 10 minutes remaining with their first back-to-back league wins at Anfield since January 1953 safely secured. Liverpool fans have reason more than most to feel aggrieved at City’s sham contracts which allowed them to inject £830m of inflated income over nine seasons, having been beaten to the title three times by their north-west rivals.

stories.title: Leinster mark RDS return with comfortable Cardiff win
stories.summary: It's business as usual for Leinster, as they marked the grand opening of their new and improved Laya Arena with a 29-5 win against Cardiff, to get up and running in the URC this season. After back-to-back defeats on their tour of South Africa, Leo Cullen’s side eased to their first victory of the campaign, as Sam Prendergast impressed in the five-try victory. The 23-year-old looked full of confidence in attack on his first start of the season and was at the heart of everything good in the Leinster performance, and there appears to be a real willingness in the out-half to bring the ball to the line, which is making both he and others a bigger attacking threat. As good as Prendergast looked with the ball in his hands, his performance off the tee will need to improve. The out-half appears to have changed the mechanics of his kicks to goal, approaching the ball more square-on, and it resulted in him missing his first three conversion attempts, two of which were sliced badly wide. All in all, it was a comfortable outing for the defending champions, who got minutes into their frontline internationals ahead of next week’s Investec Champions Cup opener against Clermont Auvergne. Four of their five tries came in the first half, as two for Jimmy O’Brien and one each for Hugo Keenan and Jack Conan had them 22-5 in front at the break, and while the second half dropoff will be a minor frustration for Cullen, they never looked in danger of being reeled in, as Jamie Osborne’s late converted try capped off the victory.

stories.title: Tom Cruise's Digger tanks, leaving studio with $250m hole
stories.summary: The Tom Cruise eco-satire Digger, a film that was supposed to herald the action hero's return to serious acting, has bombed at the box office, with industry insiders predicting it could lose a quarter of a billion dollars. The Alejandro González Iñárritu-directed comedy, starring Cruise as an eccentric oil baron who must fix the problem he has helped create, was panned by critics and has left audiences cold, leaving studio Warner Bros with a big balance sheet hole just as a merger with Paramount Skydance closes. After two weeks in cinemas, the film has grossed just $14.4 million in North America and $35.3 million globally - tiny numbers for a big-budget film that point to cumulative losses in the region of $245 million. "Financially, it has to be considered a disaster," Christopher Rosen of Hollywood trade publication The Ankler told AFP. "It cost anywhere from $160 million to $180 million - that's even before marketing - and it's made relatively nothing at the box office." Marketing for a film like Digger can cost up to $100 million.

stories.title: Read an extract of Páraic Kerrigan's 'Pop Culchie'
stories.summary:
Páraic Kerrigan's Pop Culchie: The Irish Popular Culture that Made Us is an exploration of how popular culture has shaped Irish culture and history over the last half-century. From the rise of Irish reality television and the country's first music video programme MT-USA, to forgotten chart acts, moral panics, tabloid sensations and unlikely national icons, Pop Culchie explores the stories behind the pop culture moments that defined us. Below is an extract from Chapter 2: Gas Housewives: Cookers, 'Lovely Girls' and The Calor Gas Housewife of the Year Competition. It is 1989 and on the stage of Dublin’s Olympia Theatre, Margaret Witherow, a mother of three from Convoy, Co. Donegal, stands under the bright lights beside Ireland’s beloved broadcaster Gay Byrne. As their conversation unfolds, Gay asks Margaret if she would recite a poem. Margaret, composed but a little nervous, agrees. Gay, raising an eyebrow, asks: ‘And you wrote it yourself?’ Margaret nods firmly. ‘Well done,’ Gay responds, as the room settles into a hush and Margaret begins to recite her poem, to the packed audience in the Olympia and the hundreds of thousands watching her at home on television: ‘Out of bed at seven, before I’d even yawned, a little
voice called "Mammy",
Another day had dawned.
I organised the breakfast, I was feeling none too bright,
"Mammy, have you seen my shoes, I left them here
last night."
One final check, now off you go, hurry here’s the bus,
While my easy-going husband can’t understand the fuss.
I grabbed a cup of coffee, Gaybo’s coming on,
Himself shouts from the bathroom, the sheep are on
the lawn.
I ran into the garden, still in my dressing gown,
And ran into the postman, I almost knocked him down.
He handed me a letter, another bill alas,
But no an invitation, from Calor Kosangas.
And so it was that morning, that I first got to hear,
That I had been nominated, for Housewife of the Year.’ As Margaret finishes her poem, the audience bursts into applause. Gay Byrne shakes her hand, plants a kiss on her cheek repeating, ‘Good girl, good girl’. Meanwhile, to really seal the deal, a pre-recorded segment rolls, showing Margaret’s cooking skills. She proudly presents her pièce de resistance, a leg of lamb, tastefully adorned with white heather for luck.

stories.title: Government to discuss health-led plan to tackle drug use
stories.summary: The new National Drugs Strategy for the next five years will be published after it has been approved by the Cabinet. The plan aims to tackle the harms of drug and alcohol-use through a health-led approach. The strategy will place a major emphasis on the expansion of drug treatment services in places where they are currently limited, including rural areas. Last week's Budget provided €7 million to begin implementing the strategy, which will be launched by Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill and Minister of State at the Department of Health Jennifer Murnane O'Connor. For the first time, the plan will allow gardaí to refer a person found in possession of drugs for personal use to the health services as an alternative to prosecution. The first part of the strategy will run up to 2028 and it will increase services for women, minority groups and people with additional needs.

stories.title: Picket line dilemma forces cancellation of Dáil sitting
stories.summary: This week's strike action by 300,000 public sector workers will also affect the work of politicians. It was confirmed yesterday that Wednesday’s Dáil sitting would be cancelled due to the one-day work stoppage. Leinster House workers are an integral part of the operations of the Dáil and Seanad. But as public sector employees, they are also party to the ongoing industrial action which is set to ratchet up on Wednesday with a full strike. This would mean picket lines at Leinster House, and opposition politicians immediately declared that they would not cross those lines. "The Government are intent on scheduling business when it seems clear at this stage that we will have national strikes, with the Houses of the Oireachtas impacted," said Labour Party whip Duncan Smith.

stories.title: Bumble in advanced talks to go private - source
stories.summary: Bumble is in advanced talks to be taken private by Ithaca Holdings in a deal valuing the dating app operator at roughly $1 billion, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters. Shares of the Austin, Texas-based company closed around 50% higher last night at $3.80, marking their biggest-ever percentage gain in a single session. The company had a market value of roughly $389m at Friday's close. Bumble and Ithaca, a holding company for technology businesses founded by Silicon Valley executives Ravi Gupta and John Hegeman, did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment. Reuters exclusively reported earlier this year that Bumble was exploring a sale amid slowing growth in the online dating sector. Dating apps such as Bumble and its larger rival Match Group, which owns Tinder and Hinge, have come under pressure as younger Gen Z subscribers grow disillusioned with endless swiping, leading to softer user engagement. "Going private looks less like a strategic masterstroke and more like an admission that Bumble's current strategy is failing," said PP Foresight analyst Paolo Pescatore. "A change in ownership will not magically fix these fundamental problems."

stories.summary: A secondary school pupil in France has shot and wounded a headteacher and a female staff member with a hunting rifle at a school near Marseille, causing panic as children ran for cover, the local mayor and a student said. A supervisor at Joseph Lakanal college disarmed the 14-year-old boy before police arrived, Aubagne mayor Jean-Pierre Squillari told reporters. Both victims were hospitalised, but neither suffered life-threatening injuries, he added. There was no immediate indication that the shooting was linked to a three-week wave of protests, some violent, that have rocked ‌high schools across the country. ⁠French President Emmanuel Macron condemned those incidents of violence. BFM TV said the teenager had entered the school with the rifle hidden in a guitar case. "It's a kid who goes to that school. He entered with a rifle; the investigation will determine how, and fired twice in a corridor toward the principal ‌and a teacher," Mr Squillari said.

stories.title: Hoops hold off Bohs to take command in title race
stories.summary: Dylan Watts struck a second half winner as Shamrock Rovers stretched their lead at the top of the Premier Division table to six points in seeing off arch-rivals Bohemians before a record league attendance of 10,208 at Tallaght Stadium. But a thrilling Dublin derby was unfortunately marred by unsavoury end of match scenes which saw both sets of players and backroom staff get involved in several bouts of grappling, pushing and shoving on the pitch before tempers eased and Rovers celebrated in front of their fans, Bohemians commiserating with theirs. While second-placed St Patrick's Athletic have a game in hand, it’s surely Stephen Bradley’s champions’ title to lose now as they zone in on a sixth League of Ireland pennant in seven years. Rovers finish their campaign with games away to Galway United on Friday, at home to relegated Sligo Rovers before their last day game at Dundalk. Having lost Friday’s FAI Cup seem-final to Waterford, defeat here means Bohemians’ season is all but over, although a place in next summer’s Conference League qualifiers has been secured. Alan Reynolds’ Gypsies face Waterford again at home on Friday before finishing their campaign with Dublin derbies against Shelbourne, the last game under the old Dalymount Park floodlights, and away to St Patrick’s Athletic on the final day.
